opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and honestly I think about it a lot. The common framing is that a kid sees maybe a few hundred million words before they're fluent, while we train models on trillions of tokens, so models must be wildly inefficient. I think that's partly true, but the comparison is a bit unfair in both directions.

On one side, humans don't start from scratch. There's a huge amount of prior baked in by evolution, which you could think of as a very long pretraining run that happened over millions of years. The architecture of the brain, the inductive biases, the way we're wired for language and social learning: none of that comes for free. And a child's input isn't just text. It's grounded, multimodal, interactive. You're getting vision, sound, touch, feedback from people, and you're actively choosing what to explore. That's a very different data distribution from scraping the internet and doing next-token prediction on it passively.

On the other side, I do think there's a real gap that isn't explained away by priors. Models still need to see something many, many times before it sticks, and they're not great at learning a new concept from one or two examples in a durable way. In-context learning helps, but it's not the same as actually updating your understanding of the world after a single conversation. That's where humans are still clearly better.

My practical view as someone who trains these things is that a lot of the efficiency gains have come and will keep coming from boring places: better data quality, better data mixtures, better objectives, smarter use of compute. We've seen pretty large effective-compute multipliers just from cleaning up data and picking the right mixture. Data quality is still underrated. I'm also excited about learning from interaction and feedback, because that's closer to how humans learn. RL, self-play, models generating their own training signal, getting more out of every token by doing more work per token.

So I don't think the right goal is literally matching human sample efficiency token for token. It's more about asking where the remaining inefficiency actually comes from, whether that's the objective, the data, or the lack of grounding and interaction, and then attacking those one at a time. I'd also be a little careful about assuming we need to close that gap fully to get extremely capable systems. We have a lot of data and a lot of compute, and that's been a pretty effective way of brute-forcing around the efficiency problem so far.

r001.rationale: It suggests getting more out of each token by doing more work per token, presenting greater computation per token as a way to improve model data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It mentions the brain’s architecture and inductive biases, but does not question whether limitations of the Transformer architecture contribute to the efficiency gap.

r003.rationale: It does not raise off-policy noise as a possible data-efficiency bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions I keep coming back to, and I think the honest answer is that the framing is a little bit off, or at least it's more subtle than people make it out to be.

So the standard story is: a kid sees maybe a few million words by the time they're ten, and a language model sees trillions of tokens, so humans are like three or four orders of magnitude more sample efficient. And then everyone goes, okay, there's this huge gap, we need to close it. And I think that's partially true, but it also kind of ignores a bunch of things.

The first thing is that humans aren't learning from text alone. There's a lot of multimodal grounding, there's embodiment, there's interaction, there's a teacher giving you feedback. And then there's the evolutionary prior, right? The brain isn't a randomly initialized transformer. There's a lot of architecture and inductive bias that's been "pretrained" over a very long time. So when you compare the data budget, you're not really comparing apples to apples. You're comparing a model that starts from scratch against a system that starts with a very strong prior.

The second thing is that I actually think a lot of the data we feed models is kind of... low quality, or at least redundant. Web text is super noisy. If you look at how much of the pretraining mix is actually contributing to the capabilities we care about, it's probably a small fraction. So part of the "inefficiency" is just that we're being lazy about data, because scaling has been cheap enough that we didn't have to care. When compute was the bottleneck and data was free, you just throw more data in. Now that we're starting to hit limits on high quality tokens, people are suddenly much more interested in data efficiency, curation, synthetic data, all of that. So some of the gap is going to close just because of incentives changing.

But the thing I find more interesting is the question of whether the architecture and the training objective are actually the bottleneck. Like, next token prediction is a very indirect way of learning the stuff we want. You're spending a lot of capacity modeling things that don't matter, like exact phrasing, formatting, whatever. Humans don't learn by predicting the next word in everything they hear. So there's probably a lot of headroom in objectives and in how we do things like curriculum or active learning. I've worked on a bunch of architecture stuff and my take is that architectural changes give you maybe constant factor improvements in efficiency, not order of magnitude, at least so far. The big wins have come more from data and from scale.

And then the last thing I'd say is, humans are also really bad at some things that models are great at. A model can read the entire internet. I can't. So the data efficiency comparison kind of cuts both ways. Models trade sample efficiency for breadth, and at some point that trade is actually a feature, not a bug. The real question isn't "can we make models learn like humans," it's "what's the frontier of capability per unit of data and compute," and I think we're still pretty far from the ceiling on that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data and compute tradeoffs, but does not suggest humans use greater computation per token to explain their higher data efficiency.

r002.rationale: It asks whether architecture is a bottleneck for efficiency and says architectural changes may improve it, addressing architecture limitations as a possible contributor.

r003.rationale: It calls web text noisy and redundant, but does not identify off-policy noise as a data-efficiency bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s clearly a gap, but it’s also hard to make a fair comparison. When we say a human learns something from a few examples, that person already has years of experience interacting with the world. They’re not learning from scratch. And a lot of that experience isn’t language—it’s vision, physical interaction, feedback from other people. So comparing the number of tokens a model sees with the number of words a child hears doesn’t capture everything.

That said, I do think models could be much more data efficient. The interesting question is what’s missing. Is it the learning objective? The architecture? Or the fact that humans can actively seek information, try something, and learn from what happens? A model trained on a fixed dataset doesn’t get to choose its next experience.

So I’d separate two questions: can we keep improving models by scaling the approach we have, and can we find approaches that learn more from less? I think both are worth pursuing. Progress on the first doesn’t mean we’ve solved the second.

r002.rationale: It asks whether architecture matters, but does not specifically question whether limitations of the Transformer architecture contribute to the gap.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention off-policy noise as a possible bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a pretty large gap, but it’s also hard to make that comparison cleanly. A human might learn something from a few examples, but those examples sit on top of years of experience interacting with the world. So what are we counting as the training data? It’s certainly more than the words that person has read.

That said, I think the interesting question is why models need so much repetition to pick up certain things. We train them with a fairly generic objective over huge amounts of data, whereas humans can ask questions, try something, get feedback, and focus on what they don’t understand. That’s a very different learning process.

So I’d separate two questions: how much more can we get out of the current training setup, and do we need to change the learning process itself? I think there’s room for both. Scaling has been incredibly useful, but that doesn’t mean the way we train models today is the most data-efficient way to learn.
